JAMIE: [curious] So what's the chip story? Is this just Nvidia being Nvidia, or is something deeper happening? ALEX: [sarcastic] A M D dropped seven point five two percent—that's not a wobble, that's a full retreat. Nvidia off three point nine. The narrative was supposed to be that AI infrastructure is the gold rush and everyone sells shovels and picks. Turns out the picks are getting cheaper, the competition is showing up, and the people who actually need the picks are asking harder questions about R O I. Meanwhile, Adobe up five point five five, Salesforce up five point three nine, Oracle up four point eight six—these are the companies that get to charge you monthly to use the AI they trained on your data, and nobody's questioning the math there. MAYA: [rushed] Wait, so the software companies are basically winning because they're selling the dream while hardware companies are stuck selling the reality? Like, Adobe can tell you AI will make you more creative and you just believe it, but Nvidia has to actually deliver chips that work and don't cost a fortune to run? ALEX: Exactly. One is a story that lives in a spreadsheet. The other is a supply chain that has to compete on physics and price. Guess which one Wall Street prefers today. JAMIE: [laughs] So when you said the chocolate bar margin hit a five-year high while cocoa collapsed, that was the software play. Adobe's the one sitting on the shelf at checkout while everyone else is scrambling to cut costs. MAYA: [rushed] So here's the thing nobody's talking about: Nvidia's guidance is going to be the bellwether, but what we're actually watching is whether they can still convince people that AI inference—the part where you actually *use* the model after training it—is going to be as capital-intensive as training was. Because if inference gets cheaper, the whole R O I math for enterprises flips. ALEX: [deadpan] Inference is already cheaper. That's the problem. You train on H100s, but you can run inference on older chips, smaller chips, sometimes even CPUs if you're willing to take a latency hit. Nvidia knows this. So they're going to talk about full-stack solutions, software bundles, lock-in—anything to keep the revenue per customer climbing even if the hardware margin compresses. JAMIE: [curious] Wait, so Nvidia's earnings aren't really about whether AI works. They're about whether Nvidia can convince Wall Street that Nvidia gets to own the entire chain. MAYA: [mischievously] Exactly. And that's why Meta and Microsoft and Google's earnings matter just as much. Because if those companies say 'our inference costs are dropping faster than we expected,' Nvidia has to suddenly explain why their data center revenue isn't growing as fast next quarter. It's like watching three separate earnings calls that are all secretly about the same question. ALEX: [sarcastic] Microsoft's already signaling that. They've been talking up their Maia chips and their partnerships with A M D. That's not strategy—that's insurance. They're building optionality because they know Nvidia's prices are unsustainable at current volumes. If Microsoft's capex guidance comes in flat or lower this quarter, the entire chip complex gets repriced downward. JAMIE: [excited] So earnings week isn't five separate stories. It's one story being told five different ways, and whoever breaks first—whoever admits their AI capex isn't paying off yet—that's the real headline. MAYA: And the software companies know this. They're going to report margins and user growth and act like the infrastructure underneath doesn't matter. Oracle and Salesforce don't have to answer for Nvidia's valuation. They just have to prove their AI features are sticky. That's a much easier pitch. ALEX: [deadpan] C X M T, a chipmaker, just had a market debut surge of four hundred sixty-six percent, making it the most valuable China-listed company. MAYA: [mischievously] Four hundred sixty-six percent on a company with zero distribution outside China? That's not an IPO, that's a lottery ticket printer that happens to make semiconductors. ALEX: [sarcastic] The float was probably the size of a postage stamp. You've got market cap built on what amounts to a few billion shares that actually traded hands. Pure theater—the kind where you build the entire house of cards before anyone's allowed to walk through the door. JAMIE: [curious] Cocoa futures are down from their peak, but a chocolate bar at the checkout is still expensive. So where did the savings go? ALEX: [deadpan] Into retailer margins. Chocolate makers tested the ceiling on what consumers would actually pay, found it was way higher than the input cost drop, and just... kept it. Same playbook as the tariff windfall last year—companies don't lower prices when inputs fall, they lower input costs as an excuse to raise prices elsewhere. MAYA: [rushed] So chocolate makers are basically running the C X M T playbook but in reverse: instead of announcing a product and watching the market price it into the stratosphere, they're announcing a cost collapse and watching retailers price it straight into their own pockets. JAMIE: [excited] Meta's smart glasses rollout is getting criticized for limited supply and unclear applications. MAYA: [laughs] No killer app, and the company's own AI team is more interested in chatbots than A R. So Meta's releasing hardware that solves a problem nobody has, with software that doesn't exist, to people who can't actually buy it yet. ALEX: [sarcastic] At least the market research is writing the actual headlines. JAMIE: The UK is considering shutting down Jodrell Bank, one of the world's oldest radio telescopes, to save money. MAYA: [rushed] Astronomers are saying it would tear the heart out of UK science. Which is a fancy way of saying the government is about to sell off the tools that train the next generation of researchers so they can save a budget line item for two fiscal years. ALEX: [deadpan] It's infrastructure theater. Cut the telescope, announce the savings, watch the headlines move on, and then spend three times as much rebuilding research capacity ten years later when everyone realizes you broke the pipeline. MAYA: [rushed] There's a movie called Champagne and Bullets that's now being ranked alongside The Room and Troll 2 as one of the greatest bad films ever made. JAMIE: [curious] Wait, so someone actually watched this movie, took detailed notes, and said 'yes, this belongs on the Mount Rushmore of cinematic disasters'? That's not a review, that's a historical designation. ALEX: [deadpan] The formula is always the same: ambition light-years ahead of budget, zero self-awareness, and just enough earnestness that it loops back around to being genuinely watchable. Champagne and Bullets probably cost far less than a major studio film and somehow convinced itself it was a major thriller. MAYA: [mischievously] It's the only genre where failure becomes a feature. You can't accidentally make a good action movie—but you can accidentally make a movie so committed to its own delusion that people will show up specifically to watch it collapse. JAMIE: [curious] On the tape tomorrow: Baker Hughes reports earnings, and we've got a slate of regional banks filing the same day—Sierra Bancorp, Bank of Marin, California BanCorp. Anything worth watching, or is this just the cleanup crew? ALEX: [deadpan] Baker Hughes is the one to care about. Energy services, offshore drilling, all the infrastructure plays that move with oil prices and capex cycles. If they're guiding down on rig counts or talking about margin pressure from competition, that tells you something about where energy companies think the next six months are headed. The banks are more noise—regional lenders haven't exactly been the growth story this year. MAYA: [rushed] Alpha Metallurgical Resources also reports. Coal company, which is wild because coal's supposed to be dead, but data centers and power grids are suddenly hungry again, and A M R's stock is up this year. So if they come out and say 'yeah, we're actually printing money because everyone needs baseload power for AI servers,' that's the real story nobody saw coming. JAMIE: [excited] So we've got the energy infrastructure play, the regional banking check-in, and the coal company that became relevant again by accident. ALEX: [sarcastic] Broadcom up three point four-six percent, A M D up three point five percent. These are the companies that benefit from a weaker dollar and a Fed pivot in the same breath. Cisco's down three point six-eight percent because nobody's buying networking gear when they're too busy watching the Fed move the furniture. ALEX: [sarcastic] And here's what the market's not pricing in: Morgan Stanley's fixed income trading revenue actually fell. Bonds are boring when everyone thinks rates are about to drop—nobody needs to hedge, nobody's scared, the vol just evaporates. JAMIE: [laughs] So the market's not celebrating Morgan Stanley's earnings, it's celebrating that the fear trade finally switched off. MAYA: Which means next quarter, when the Fed doesn't cut and traders realize they've been front-running a speech, Morgan Stanley's equities desk is going to post numbers that look like a typo. The bank's stock will crater, and everyone will act shocked that a quarter built entirely on one-directional betting didn't hold up. JAMIE: [curious] Warren Buffett on the market today: 'It's tough to find values when everybody is preferring gambling.' ALEX: [deadpan] When Buffett says he can't find value, he means the marginal dollar in the market is not interested in cash flows or balance sheets. It's interested in whether the Fed moves the furniture. That's not a market correction—that's a market that's stopped being a market. MAYA: [rushed] A SpaceX vet just raised sixty-five million dollars to modernize wire harnesses—the literal cables that hold rockets together. Nobody's funding this because it's sexy, they're funding it because every aerospace company is still using wiring diagrams from the eighties. JAMIE: [laughs] So there's a company that builds AI models worth billions, and there's a company that bundles wires for satellites, and the wire company just got sixty-five million because the infrastructure is so broken that fixing it is the actual venture. MAYA: [excited] Anthropic and Blackstone are betting the next trillion-dollar AI business isn't building the model—it's embedding engineers inside enterprises to actually make the thing work. ALEX: [sarcastic] So the narrative's shifting from 'we built a smarter G P T' to 'we hired someone to sit in your finance department and make sure the smarter G P T doesn't hallucinate your tax return.' That's not a product, that's a consulting firm with a neural network. JAMIE: PayPal's stock is soaring on rumors that Stripe and Advent Capital are circling for a buyout. A company that used to own the entire future of payments is now a takeover target. MAYA: [mischievously] PayPal spent the last five years trying to convince everyone they were still relevant, and the market's answer is: sure, but only if someone else buys you. MAYA: [rushed] The UK government just proposed a midnight social media curfew for sixteen and seventeen-year-olds—which sounds like a real policy until you read the fine print and realize teenagers can just opt out. Apple's up four point eight four percent, Netflix up four point six six, Adobe up four point one four—all the stuff that actually makes revenue. Meanwhile Tesla's down seven point four nine percent on delivery concerns, Meta's down four point nine on the AI delay we just covered. The mega-cap AI narrative is getting sorted into 'hardware and software that works' versus 'we spent a hundred billion dollars and the thing isn't ready.' JAMIE: [curious] So the market's saying Apple knows how to ship a phone but Meta doesn't know how to ship an agent. That's a brutal split. MAYA: [rushed] And Tesla's getting hammered separately—not even the AI story, just delivery numbers coming in soft. But here's the thing: Accenture's up four point seven four percent, McDonald's up four point one six, Cisco down three point six nine. The market's rewarding boring competence right now. You can sell cloud infrastructure to banks, you can sell franchises burgers, you can't sell 'trust us, the AI agents are coming next quarter.' Gold's up because apparently everyone needs a security blanket. JAMIE: [laughs] So we've got this weird moment where the V I X dropped below sixteen—that's calm—but investors are basically saying 'I believe in your products, not your promises.' Apple's promise is a phone you can hold. Meta's promise is... software that doesn't exist yet. MAYA: [rushed] So Zuckerberg's in this all-hands, right, and he just—casually drops that the AI agents roadmap is slipping. Not 'we're optimizing timelines,' not 'we're taking a more thoughtful approach'—he said they haven't progressed as quickly as he'd hoped. Which is CEO-speak for 'I promised this would be here by now and it is not here.' ALEX: [deadpan] And the reason that matters is Meta's already committed to spending on capital expenditure—mostly data centers and chips to train these agents. That money's already allocated. The agents aren't delivering the returns he said they would. So you're locked into the spending, but the payoff just moved to a date nobody knows yet. JAMIE: [curious] Is he saying the technology isn't working, or is he saying it's working but slower to deploy at scale? Because those are different problems. MAYA: [mischievously] He didn't get specific—and that's the tell. If it was just a deployment bottleneck, he'd say 'we're ramping production next quarter.' Instead he said progress hasn't been quick enough, which means the R&D itself is grinding. OpenAI's shipping G P T-4o, Anthropic's shipping Claude, Google's shipping Gemini, and Meta's apparently in a room going 'so about those agents we've been training on compute...' ALEX: [deadpan] Gold's up for the first week in a month as investors are pulling back on Fed rate-hike bets—the market's pricing in a pause now, not cuts, which is a subtle shift but it moves the needle on what central banks are actually allowed to do. JAMIE: [curious] So the Fed's still holding, but the market's stopped betting they'll keep tightening? ALEX: [deadpan] Exactly. The inflation data's not screaming anymore, and traders are reading that as 'okay, maybe we're done here,' which is why gold's rallying—it doesn't pay interest, so it only wins when real rates are expected to stay low or fall. MAYA: [rushed] A politician in Europe who was investigating spyware abuses had his phone hacked with Pegasus spyware—which is either the most poetic irony or a threat so direct it doesn't even need words. JAMIE: [laughs] Wait, so the tool used to hack him was the same one he was investigating? MAYA: [mischievously] Yes. The politician was looking into spyware abuses, and some government just decided to make his investigation personal. It's like hiring a private investigator to prove you're not being investigated. ALEX: [sarcastic] Ford's CEO just announced the automaker is targeting flawless vehicle launches after years of quality recalls—which means the bar used to be 'doesn't spontaneously fail,' and now it's 'perfection,' so either they've figured something out or they're setting themselves up for the most visible failure in automotive history. JAMIE: [excited] Europe's top bankers and regulators are warning that AI is already outpacing the rules they're supposed to write, which translates to: we have no framework for this, we will create one anyway, and it will probably be obsolete before it's finalized. MAYA: [rushed] So there's a literary AI scandal where a writer's use of AI tools in the writing process sent people into a frenzy about authenticity and craft and whether a machine learning model can have a muse. Now he's coming forward with his version of what actually happened, and it turns out the story people were mad about isn't the story he was living. JAMIE: [curious] Hold on—so the controversy was premature? People decided he cheated before he even got a chance to explain what he did? ALEX: [deadpan] The literary establishment is spending real energy right now deciding whether a tool that predicts the next word counts as collaboration or theft, which is genuinely harder to solve than any of the AI regulation Europe's supposedly writing. At least with spyware everyone agrees hacking someone's phone is bad. With this, half the internet thinks AI in the writing process is the future and the other half thinks it's the death of literature, and the writer's just standing there holding a prize that nobody can agree he deserved. MAYA: [rushed] Meta's going to spend the next earnings call explaining why a major bet on agents is actually a down payment on the future, not a sunk cost they're trying to justify. ALEX: [deadpan] By which time the market will have already decided whether it believes the next date they give us. JAMIE: This show is for entertainment and education only — nothing here is investment advice.

item.ns2:encoded: JAMIE: [excited] Meta's down three point two seven percent today, but yesterday it jumped ten percent—turns out the real business model is just renting your AI compute to everyone else. ALEX: [deadpan] So yesterday we're all marveling at Meta's compute arbitrage—sell it to everyone, undercut cloud providers, pocket the margin spread. Except margin spread assumes you're not also burning money on data centers. It's like finding spare change in your couch and deciding you've solved your mortgage problem. Wall Street realized that giving away your infrastructure at cost while your core business cools is not a growth strategy. ALEX: [deadpan] Markets are up across the board today—S&P at seven thousand five hundred thirty-six, up zero point seven one percent, Nasdaq at twenty-six thousand two hundred forty-eight, up zero point eight. V I X collapsed four point one percent down to fifteen point ninety-one, which means investors decided overnight that the jobs report was soft enough to buy everything. Apple's up two point eight nine percent, Accenture up two point eight two, Adobe up two point seven seven. Then you've got Meta down three point two seven and Tesla down three point two five—both getting absolutely hammered. JAMIE: [curious] So the market's basically celebrating that the economy might be slowing down enough that the Fed won't keep rates where they are. And Meta's being punished for yesterday's compute arbitrage story because Wall Street realized it doesn't actually work if you're bleeding money a year. But Tesla—why is Tesla down alongside Meta? Those are completely different stories. MAYA: [rushed] Tesla's probably just getting caught in the rotation out of mega-cap growth. But also there could be supply chain rumors, or—honestly, at this point Tesla moves on vibes. Meanwhile, the actual winners today are Oracle up two point three four percent, Broadcom, Lilly up one point seven nine. So you've got cloud infrastructure and pharma doing well on the softer rate story, which makes sense. ALEX: [sarcastic] Right. And the V I X crash and a rally would normally push yields down. But instead we're getting both—yields up, stocks up, V I X down. That only happens when the market is repricing growth expectations and rate expectations at the same time. JAMIE: [laughs] So we're in a world where softer employment means the Fed might cut, and that's bullish for equities and crypto. It's not recession anxiety—it's just Goldilocks anxiety. MAYA: [excited] And the dollar's down, which is the one thing that makes sense if you're expecting rate cuts. Weaker dollar means emerging markets get cheaper, commodities get cheaper in dollar terms. So the entire machine is working the way it's supposed to for once, which is probably why nobody's panicking and the V I X is sleeping. MAYA: [rushed] The real problem here is that Meta's cloud play doesn't just add a revenue line—it cannibalizes the margins on the revenue they already have. They're not renting spare compute capacity on weekends. They're building this infrastructure to undercut Amazon Web Services and Google Cloud on price, which means they're competing on a margin that's lower than what they're making on ads. ALEX: [deadpan] Right, and Wall Street's math on this is still stuck in the old model. Cloud infrastructure runs at lower margins than advertising. So the question isn't whether they can win market share—it's whether shareholders are willing to watch their margin profile get shredded while they build this thing out. JAMIE: [curious] But Zuckerberg's already committed to this. He's got significant capex planned. That's not a test project. That's a bet-the-company infrastructure spend. So either this works and Meta becomes a cloud player with lower margins, or it doesn't work and they've just spent money to lose the advertising margin game to nobody. MAYA: [mischievously] And here's the thing nobody's talking about—Meta's already selling compute to other companies through their Llama models and their AI partnerships. They're not starting from zero. But the minute they go after A W S's enterprise customers directly, they're in a price war with a company that's been doing this for years and has the relationships locked in. It's like deciding to compete with Coca-Cola by buying a soda fountain. ALEX: [sarcastic] The second-order problem is that if Meta succeeds at cloud, they're also training Nvidia's replacement. Every dollar of Meta's cloud revenue is a dollar that doesn't go to Nvidia's data center business. Nvidia's already priced for Meta, Google, and Microsoft's capex to stay elevated forever. If Meta becomes the distributor instead of just the buyer, Nvidia's growth story gets a lot more complicated. JAMIE: [laughs] So the market's not actually punishing Meta because the cloud strategy is stupid. It's punishing them because the market finally realizes that margin compression is real, and the people who make the chips are more valuable than the people who rent the chips. MAYA: [rushed] AutoCamp just raised capital to expand their glamping empire—Airstream suites, design-forward fire pits, the whole aspirational outdoor thing. They're charging premium rates for a very nice tent, but the business model is essentially 'what if we took the part of camping where you're uncomfortable and charged you premium rates to experience it?' JAMIE: [curious] Wait, so they're not actually selling the experience of being outside. They're selling the photograph of being outside. You show up, you get the Instagram moment, the Airstream is immaculate, the fire pit is Instagram-optimized, and then you're back in a climate-controlled bedroom by nine p.m. That's not camping. That's theater with a sleeping bag. ALEX: [deadpan] The unit economics are actually interesting because they're not fighting over land costs the way hotels do. They're buying established destinations and dropping branded infrastructure on them. So the margin profile works if occupancy stays high and they can scale the operational footprint without proportional headcount growth. The capital raise is probably funding that replication play across new geographies. MAYA: [mischievously] Except they're still operating at the mercy of weather and seasonal demand. You can't Uber Eats your way out of a rainy July. And the second you try to raise prices or cut amenities, you're not a luxury brand anymore—you're just a motel that refused to install walls. They're betting that people will keep paying premium rates to sleep outside if the pillows are expensive enough. ALEX: [deadpan] Meta's margin story is like a magic trick where you finally see the trapdoor. The rabbit was never really there. MAYA: [mischievously] So we're all just watching them build the stage to disappoint us slower. JAMIE: This show is for entertainment and education only — nothing here is investment advice.

MAYA: [rushed] The thing that's actually wild is the comparison to SpaceX—both companies built massive infrastructure for their primary mission, SpaceX for rockets and Meta for training AI models, but SpaceX already had a playbook when they started launching services. Meta is out here going, 'Wait, we have a data center problem? Let's become a cloud provider.' It's not a plan, it's a fire sale of capacity. ALEX: [deadpan] Right, but the infrastructure cost is already sunk. At that point, you're not losing money by renting it out—you're just printing margin on something that's already built and humming. The question is whether they can actually compete with Amazon, Google, and Microsoft on service, not on hardware. JAMIE: [curious] But those three have been doing this for over a decade. They've got customer relationships, compliance frameworks, the whole stack. Meta's got excess GPUs and a reputation for privacy disasters. How does that pitch meeting even go? MAYA: [mischievously] They lead with price and speed. Meta can undercut on compute cost because they don't need to build a business around it—it's a byproduct. And they've already got relationships with thousands of app developers from the Meta ecosystem. The real threat isn't that Meta becomes the cloud leader; it's that they become a viable alternative for companies that don't want to be locked into A W S or Azure. That alone fractures the oligopoly a little. ALEX: [sarcastic] Except the major cloud providers make substantial revenue and run at strong operating margins. Meta's cloud business doesn't exist yet. They'd need to hire teams, build support infrastructure, deal with SLAs and enterprise contracts. That's not a byproduct—that's a business. And it bleeds cash while they're learning. JAMIE: [laughs] So the market's pricing in that Meta figured out how to turn a cost center into a profit center, but the bear case is they're about to learn that cloud services aren't just 'rent out your spare GPUs and call it a day.' They have to actually run a business. MAYA: [excited] And if they stumble, they're still burning significant capex on AI that's not generating enough revenue to justify it. So the stock gets punished twice—once for the cloud play failing, once for the core AI bet looking like a black hole. That's the real risk no one's talking about. MAYA: [rushed] Getty and Shutterstock's merger is officially dead—the US cleared it, but the UK regulators blocked it hard enough that both companies just walked away. ALEX: [deadpan] So the US looked at the deal, saw no monopoly problem, and the UK looked at the exact same deal and said it would crush competition in image licensing. Two regulators, one transaction, opposite conclusions. JAMIE: [curious] Which means if you're a CEO trying to do a cross-border deal, you now have to clear every single regulatory jurisdiction separately, and if one says no, the whole thing dies anyway. That's not merger arbitrage—that's a regulatory lottery where losing one ticket kills the prize. ALEX: [sarcastic] Warsh says the Fed will hint at rate moves only when they 'shut the door' at the next meeting—which in central bank language means they're not telling anyone anything until they've already decided. JAMIE: [laughs] So the entire market is supposed to just sit in silence until the Fed walks into a room, closes the door, and then tells everyone what they decided. That's not transparency—that's a surprise party where the guest of honor is inflation. MAYA: [excited] Venice AI just hit unicorn status on sixty-five million in Series A funding, and the pitch is basically 'we train AI models without stealing your data'—which is apparently a contrarian move. ALEX: [deadpan] They're already doing strong revenue and they're profitable. So they built a business first and got valued as a unicorn second, which is the opposite of every other AI startup that got the valuation first and is still figuring out what the business is. JAMIE: [laughs] England just had its warmest June on record, which means London tech conferences are now a legitimate occupational hazard. MAYA: [mischievously] So basically everyone's pretending to care about climate while sweating through their keynotes. MAYA: [rushed] Rhythm Heaven just dropped a new game on Switch—first entry in the series since 2012, and before this week there were only four games total, one of which never left Japan. Nintendo let this franchise sit dormant for over a decade and then just dropped it like nothing happened, no marketing blitz, no lead-up. It's the most Nintendo thing possible: ignore a cult classic until you remember it exists, then release it. JAMIE: [curious] So they had a loyal audience waiting twelve years and didn't even tease it? That's not confidence—that's negligence disguised as mystery. ALEX: [deadpan] Rhythm Heaven's whole thing is that your timing has to be pixel-perfect or the game makes you feel like you have no rhythm at all. It's basically a device that proves most people shouldn't be allowed near percussion instruments. The fact that they're bringing it back now, when everyone's playing other games, is like reopening a restaurant that only serves foods you can't chew properly. MAYA: [mischievously] But that's exactly why it works—Rhythm Heaven doesn't need hype because the game itself is the punishment. You boot it up, miss one beat, and spend the next six minutes convinced your brain is broken. That's the marketing. That's the viral moment. Your friends watching you fail is the product. MAYA: [rushed] Meta's about to learn that excess capacity and actual customer service are not the same thing. ALEX: [deadpan] In other words, they're about to hire a thousand support engineers to tell people their model crashed at 2 A M. JAMIE: [curious] Wait—so we're simultaneously discovering that the infrastructure they're building on requires... permits and zoning boards? ALEX: [deadpan] A data center in Iowa needs more water than the town's municipal supply. JAMIE: [laughs] So we're in a moment where Procter & Gamble is down two point six-six because it sells soap, but nobody's panicking that the entire AI infrastructure boom depends on getting a zoning variance approved in Nebraska. ALEX: [deadpan] Here's what Warsh actually changed: the Fed had been signaling for months that if things got weird, there's a floor. Now he's saying the Fed is stepping back from that deal. Not dramatically—it's a posture shift, not a policy reversal—but the market's already reading it as 'central bank puts are off.' And the weird part is, that's not making everything cheaper. It's making the expensive stuff more expensive because there's no safety net underneath volatility anymore. JAMIE: [curious] Wait, so the removal of the safety net is making equities go up? The market's saying 'if there's no put, then we need to be even more concentrated in the things that don't need a put'—which is why certain stocks keep getting bid up while everything else gets repriced. It's like the Fed just told the market 'you can take as much leverage as you want' and the market immediately took that as 'we should lever up into the only stocks we're sure about.' Once the Fed stops being the bagholder of last resort, the market has to price in actual default risk for the first time in years. Companies like Accenture—or any mid-cap that's been living on the assumption that the Fed would never let things get that bad—they're suddenly trading on fundamentals. Not hype, not 'the Fed's got my back,' just 'can you actually make money?' Warsh isn't raising rates. He's just removing the implicit guarantee that volatility will be managed for you. MAYA: [rushed] It's going to be noise for three weeks and then someone's going to write a 'why the Iran deal is actually bullish for AI infrastructure' thread and we'll all have to pretend that made sense. ALEX: [sarcastic] Software fix, not hardware, so the cars themselves are fine. They just need to be taught that when humans put giant neon warnings on the road, that's a signal to not drive there. ALEX: [sarcastic] Except 'deal cycles are lengthening' is Wall Street speak for 'our customers are scared and our sales team can't close anything.' SentinelOne's guidance is basically 'somewhere between growth and contraction.' They're hedging so hard they might as well have said 'we have no idea what happens in ninety days.' The business works, the market just doesn't believe in the future anymore. MAYA: [rushed] So they beat on the past and got punished for the future. This stock has commitment issues. It's like saying 'I made great money last year, but I'm genuinely unsure if I'll make money next year,' and the market goes 'okay we're out.' How many other security companies are seeing the same thing? ALEX: [sighs] The whole cybersecurity space is basically pricing in a spending freeze right now. Investors aren't asking 'is the product good?' anymore. They're asking 'will the CFO actually sign the check?' and the answer from SentinelOne was 'we're not sure.' JAMIE: [laughs] So this is the real test of the soft landing narrative. If cybersecurity—which is supposed to be non-discretionary, recession-proof spending—is getting deferred, then we're not in a soft landing. We're in a 'companies are acting like a hard landing is coming' landing. MAYA: [mischievously] Exactly. SentinelOne didn't lose a customer. It just lost the market's faith that it will gain any new ones. And if security spending is optional now, nothing is mandatory anymore. [rushed] Wikipedia editors are threatening to strike over AI training data—and I mean the people who literally built the internet's most trusted source are about to unionize against the thing that's supposed to make them obsolete. JAMIE: [curious] Wait, how many editors are we talking about here? This isn't like a fringe group. MAYA: [excited] Hundreds of prolific editors—the people who actually maintain the thing. And the issue is that Wikimedia started letting AI companies train on Wikipedia content without compensation or even a heads-up to the people who wrote it. So basically the institution said 'we're monetizing your unpaid labor' and the volunteers said 'no.' ALEX: [deadpan] So Wikipedia chose to become the training data for every large language model while the people maintaining it get nothing, and now those people are saying they'll delete their contributions if it doesn't stop. That's the digital equivalent of a factory worker threatening to dismantle the machines they built. JAMIE: [laughs] And here's the thing—Wikipedia is one of the last places on the internet where you can actually trust the information. If the editors walk, the whole thing becomes just another dataset, not a community project. Wikimedia basically bet that the editors had nowhere else to go. ALEX: [sarcastic] Gas prices are dropping—but they're still high, which is the economic equivalent of 'we fixed it but didn't fix it.' Consumer relief theater with an asterisk. MAYA: [mischievously] So people are supposed to feel better because gas went down from the peak, but it's still brutal. That's not a win, that's just less losing. JAMIE: [curious] Trump's one point seven seven billion dollar anti-weaponization fund just got blocked by a federal judge—which means the administration chose violence today and lost in court before lunch. ALEX: [deadpan] The fund was temporarily blocked. So the whole thing is on hold. This is what happens when you try to turn the government into a political piggy bank. MAYA: [rushed] And the timing is wild because they're trying to do this while simultaneously arguing they're not weaponizing the government. The judge basically said 'you can't call it an anti-weaponization fund if it's literally just paying off political allies.' ALEX: [sighs] Fed Governor Michelle Bowman just warned against hiking interest rates on top of the inflation spike—and here's the thing: she's a governor actively arguing against the Fed's own playbook, which means the institution is fracturing in real time. JAMIE: [excited] So Bowman is saying energy prices and tariffs are driving inflation, and hiking rates won't fix that—it'll just crush growth. And she's right. But the fact that a Fed governor is publicly dissenting this hard means the consensus is breaking. MAYA: [rushed] Infinity Ward just announced the next Call of Duty is set in a North Korean invasion scenario. So basically Activision looked at the current geopolitical situation and decided what the market really needed was a playable version of the thing that might actually happen. JAMIE: [laughs] Wait, so they're launching a game about North Korea invading while actual tensions are spiking? That's either the most tone-deaf product launch in gaming history or the most prescient—either way, Activision is betting that geopolitical instability is a feature, not a bug. They're selling anxiety as entertainment. ALEX: [deadpan] The game is supposed to be grounded in military authenticity, which is corporate speak for 'we did just enough research to sound credible while making sure you can still quickscope a general.' Activision spent millions making sure the weapons feel real and the scenario feels plausible, but the actual geopolitical context? That's just ambient flavor. It's like selling a recession simulator and calling it 'educational gaming.' MAYA: [mischievously] So in six months, if tensions actually escalate, Activision gets free marketing because millions of people have already run through the scenario in their living room. And if nothing happens, they just sold a game where you get to feel like a soldier. Either way, they're not losing sleep—they're just monetizing your fear of what might be coming. [sarcastic] So we're going to hear 'strong execution, uncertain outlook' from every CFO for the next twelve months, and investors will just keep selling on the news. Defensive stocks are rallying like the apocalypse is scheduled for Thursday. Meanwhile, JPMorgan is down three point four two percent, which tracks with Jamie's opening—Dimon's twenty billion dollar war chest announcement apparently spooked people. [deadpan] Nothing says "we have a plan" like losing market cap before lunch. JAMIE: [laughs] Wait, so the market saw JPMorgan's massive cash position and thought, "Hmm, sounds like they're worried about something." That's the financial equivalent of your friend saying they just got a really good deal on a bunker. ALEX: Exactly. And it's not just JPMorgan. Semiconductors are getting demolished—A M D down two point eight eight, Nvidia down two point four seven. The V I X is actually falling, down point four seven, which is the deadpan part—volatility's calm but everything expensive is selling off. [sarcastic] This is what happens when you have a market that's simultaneously decided "risk is over" and "growth is suspicious." MAYA: [rushed] So hold on, hold on—Procter & Gamble up three point three five percent while Nvidia's bleeding? That's not a rotation, that's a full evacuation. [excited] People are literally running from the future and into consumer staples. ALEX: [sighs] The dollar's barely moving, but crude's down. Oil's actually the only thing that makes sense today. Are we in a "soft landing confirmed" moment, or is this just people panic-hedging into staples because they think something's coming? MAYA: [rushed, excited] Okay, so there's a database company called ClickHouse that just tripled its annualized revenue to two hundred fifty million dollars, and literally nobody outside of infrastructure nerds knows who they are. Two hundred fifty million. That's not a side project—that's a real business that's apparently been printing money in the shadows while we've all been obsessed with AI chatbots. JAMIE: [curious] Wait, ClickHouse? I've genuinely never heard of this company. What do they actually do? MAYA: [mischievously] They make a database that's really fast at analyzing massive amounts of data. Think of it as an alternative to other data warehouse solutions—no venture capital theater, just a project that somehow convinced enterprises to pay them a quarter billion dollars a year. ALEX: [deadpan] A quarter billion dollars in A R R and we're on turn three of a podcast beat. That's the actual story here—this is what happens when you build something useful instead of something that requires a T E D talk to explain. JAMIE: [laughs] So the market's obsessed with Nvidia and AI infrastructure plays, but the actual infrastructure that makes AI work—the databases—is just quietly becoming a monster business? MAYA: [excited] Exactly. And here's the absurd part—they're eyeing an IPO within the next few years, which means they're probably already at a significant valuation, and Wall Street's going to pretend they discovered this company yesterday. ALEX: [sighs] The database market is genuinely massive—we're talking hundreds of billions in total addressable market—and it's one of the few enterprise software categories where you can actually have a profitable, growing business without needing to convince investors you're going to replace human consciousness. ClickHouse's two hundred fifty million A R R is probably doing better margins than most SaaS companies at twice the revenue. JAMIE: [curious] So when they do go public, what's the actual pitch? Is it "we're the boring, profitable alternative," or do they get caught up in the same hype cycle? MAYA: [rushed, mischievously] They're going to try to position themselves as the "open-source, community-driven, anti-establishment database play," which will last approximately four minutes into the investor roadshow before someone asks about AI capabilities and suddenly they're claiming their database is essential for various enterprise applications. [laughs] This stock has commitment issues—it'll either be valued like a boring infrastructure company or hyped like the next big thing, and there's no in-between. ALEX: [deadpan] The real tell is going to be the IPO price. If they price it at a reasonable multiple to revenue, then we know the market's actually functioning. If it's much higher and they're calling themselves "the AI database," then we're back to a situation where nobody understands what's happening, but the momentum's real, so we're all just along for the ride. Abercrombie & Fitch is up thirteen percent on an earnings beat, which would be great except sales in certain regions dropped because of the Iran conflict. [deadpan] So the market saw "we crushed expectations" and completely ignored "our actual business is shrinking in affected areas." This stock has commitment issues. ALEX: [sarcastic] Cost-cutting and margin expansion in the regions that still exist. It's the financial equivalent of saying your restaurant's doing great because you fired half the staff and stopped buying fresh ingredients. The headline won the day. MAYA: [rushed] Okay, but Foot Locker's actually back to growth, right? Dick's Sporting Goods acquired them and now Dick's is down because the turnaround's expensive. JAMIE: [laughs] So the market's like, "I respect the acquisition strategy, but I'm going to punish you for actually executing it." MAYA: [mischievously, rushed] Okay, Iran's internet shutdown just ended, and Iranians are describing it like being released from prison. [excited] That's not just a connectivity story—that's a freedom story. The government cut them off during the conflict, and now they're back online and everyone's just trying to catch up on what the world did without them. ALEX: [sighs] The New York Fed just reported a remarkable increase in food insecurity, which is Fed-speak for "we're genuinely shocked this is happening while the stock market's at all-time highs." [deadpan] The S&P's ripping, Coca-Cola's rallying, and apparently millions of Americans are skipping meals. That tracks. JAMIE: [curious] What's the actual number on food insecurity from the Fed? ALEX: They reported a remarkable increase, but the specific percentage wasn't detailed in the initial report. [sarcastic] When the New York Fed says something's remarkable, it means it's actually remarkable. MAYA: [rushed, excited] Okay, Ferrari just launched a new all-electric vehicle, and the Ferrari fan community is absolutely dunking on it. Like, we're talking highly upvoted Reddit threads comparing it to other vehicles. One commenter said it "looks like what happens when you ask ChatGPT to design a sports car," and that's the nicest thing anyone's said about it. JAMIE: [curious] Wait, Ferrari's first E V looks like other vehicles? How does that even happen? They've had a hundred years to figure out what a Ferrari looks like. ALEX: [deadpan] The vehicle is an all-electric model that looks like someone told Ferrari's design team, "Make it practical," and they responded by removing every distinguishing feature the brand's ever had. It's the automotive equivalent of a startup that raised hundreds of millions of dollars to solve a problem nobody had—except in this case, the problem was "how do we make a Ferrari that nobody wants to drive?" MAYA: [mischievously, laughs] The worst part is Ferrari's trying to position this as the future of the brand, which means in five years they're going to have multiple electric models in every color, and actual Ferrari enthusiasts are just going to start buying used models from decades past because at least those looked like something worth the price. [deadpan] If he actually deploys twenty billion, it'll be the most aggressive M&A spree in banking since 2008, but odds are we're watching banker theater where the real play is keeping the cash on the balance sheet and pretending optionality is a strategy. MAYA: [rushed, mischievously] The thing that kills me is JPMorgan's already the biggest bank in America—like, they don't need to buy anything, they're just doing this because Dimon's bored and has a competitive complex about being smaller than his own institution's ambitions. [laughs] It's the corporate equivalent of someone who's already won the game deciding to play on hard mode just to feel something. item.ns2:encoded: JAMIE: Walmart stock just tanked seven point three nine percent because the company wants to give you cheaper groceries—and Wall Street is genuinely mad about it. ALEX: S&P down zero point three three percent, Nasdaq down zero point four eight percent, and the Russell two thousand actually up zero point one six percent—which is the market's way of saying "we're scared of big tech but we'll take whatever we can get." Walmart lost seven point three nine percent. Adobe down three point eight six percent. Costco down two point six six percent. Meanwhile Cisco jumped two point one eight percent, which tells you everything: investors are fleeing growth and hugging infrastructure like it's a life raft. JAMIE: [curious] So Walmart tanks because it wants to help people afford groceries, and Cisco moons because—what, they sell the boring pipes that hold the internet together? ALEX: [deadpan] Exactly. Walmart chose violence today against its own margin. Cisco is basically the Crocs IPO of corporate governance—nobody's excited about it, but it works, it's profitable, and apparently that's enough to make money right now. The V I X dropped to seventeen point three five, so macro anxiety eased, but earnings reality is biting. Tech and retail are both getting their teeth kicked in because the market finally realized growth stocks need to, you know, grow. MAYA: [rushed, excited] Wait, so Cisco is just—it's the safe choice? That's the trade? We're in a world where A M D is down two percent and Cisco is up because it's boring? [laughs] That's not a market, that's a nursing home portfolio. ALEX: [sarcastic] Welcome to 2025, where the exciting part of the stock market is watching companies that sell switches to data centers. Netflix up one point three three percent, Merck up one point three nine percent, Eli Lilly up one point five eight percent—these are your winners. You know what they have in common? None of them promised to disrupt anything. JAMIE: [laughs] So the Walmart thing—that stock has commitment issues. They say "we want lower prices," the market says "no," they panic. Meanwhile Cisco's just sitting there like "I will do the same thing I did in two thousand and three" and Wall Street throws money at it. MAYA: [rushed, excited] Okay so SpaceX just filed its S-one for the Nasdaq listing, and the filing is basically screaming one thing: Starlink is not a side project, Starlink is the entire business. Like, Starlink generated the majority of SpaceX's revenue growth, and the prospectus literally says the company is "dependent on Starlink for growth and profitability." Elon's not going to Mars on rocket money—he's going to Mars on satellite internet money. JAMIE: [curious] Wait, so the company that's supposed to be about launching rockets to space is actually making its money by... beaming the internet from space back down to your house in Nebraska? ALEX: [deadpan] Yes. SpaceX's core business—the thing that gets venture capitalists and defense contractors excited—is the Falcon nine and Falcon Heavy launches. But Starlink is where the cash is. The filing doesn't give exact numbers, but the rocket business is still burning money on development and government contracts. [sighs] This is what happens when your founder gets bored with the original mission. MAYA: [mischievously] It's like if Tesla filed for IPO and the prospectus said "by the way, we make most of our money selling solar panels to Costco, not cars." Investors bought the Mars story. They're getting the Starlink story. JAMIE: [laughs] But hold on—is that actually bad? Like, if Starlink is profitable and growing, why would Wall Street care that it's not the rocket division? ALEX: [sarcastic] Because Wall Street bought a ticket to Mars and got a fiber optic cable. Starlink is a telecommunications business. It has competition—Amazon's got Project Kuiper launching soon, and unlike Elon, Amazon actually has the cash to burn. Starlink has a foothold. And the prospectus basically admits the company's future depends on whether Starlink can scale faster than Amazon can copy it. MAYA: [excited] Plus there's the whole thing where Starlink is also SpaceX's biggest customer for launches. Like, SpaceX launches Starlink satellites, Starlink pays SpaceX for the launches, and then SpaceX reports both as revenue. [laughs] It's not circular exactly, but it's definitely... cozy. The filing has to disclose that Starlink accounted for over fifty percent of SpaceX's launch revenue. JAMIE: [curious] So when SpaceX goes public, we're basically buying a bet on satellite internet, not a bet on Mars rockets? ALEX: You're buying a bet on whether Elon can execute two businesses at once without one of them imploding. The rocket division is government-dependent—it's got contracts with the Air Force, N A S A, the Space Force. That's stable. But it's also heavily regulated and capped by how many launches the government needs. Starlink is the growth story. Starlink is also the thing that could get crushed by Amazon, or by regulatory pushback. [deadpan] The filing doesn't mention the collision problem, but it's there. MAYA: [rushed] And here's the thing—the IPO is valued at a significant amount or more, right? That valuation is built on Starlink being the next generation of internet infrastructure. But if you strip out Starlink, SpaceX is just a launch provider. A really good one, but a launch provider. The margins on that are okay, not transformational. You're not going public on "we launch rockets reliably." You're going public on "we're going to wire the entire planet with internet from space." JAMIE: [laughs] So Elon's basically saying, "I know I said I was going to colonize Mars, but first let me make sure everyone in rural Wyoming can stream TikTok." That's not a pivot, that's a full one-eighty. ALEX: [sarcastic] It's the Crocs IPO of space companies. Nobody thought Starlink would be the profit engine. Everyone thought it was the cool vanity project. Turns out the vanity project is the only thing that works. MAYA: Anthropic is paying fifteen billion dollars a year for access to data centers while SpaceX is literally filing to go public right now. [rushed, excited] This is the Crocs IPO of corporate governance. The CEO's side hustle becomes the main character. JAMIE: [curious] Wait, so Anthropic needs compute to train Claude, and they're basically funding infrastructure while a company is about to ask public markets for capital? ALEX: [deadpan] Yes. Anthropic just handed a company fifteen billion a year in guaranteed revenue—which can now be put in the prospectus as "recurring enterprise customer revenue." The filing doesn't need to say "we have one customer paying us fifteen billion," but it can imply the data center business is scaled and real. [sighs] The funding helped the IPO story. MAYA: [mischievously] It's like if you lent your friend money to buy a house, and then he immediately listed the house on Zillow and told the bank "see, I have income." ALEX: Air France and Airbus were just convicted of manslaughter by a French court over a plane crash—two hundred twenty-eight people died, and it took years to get a guilty verdict. [deadpan] Turns out "too big to fail" doesn't mean "too big to prosecute." JAMIE: [curious] So a court actually held a major airline and a major aircraft manufacturer criminally liable? That doesn't happen. ALEX: It happened in France. The court found Air France negligent for not detecting a known issue with the air speed sensor, and Airbus negligent for not warning operators about the sensor's failure mode. They each got fined five million euros. [sarcastic] Which for Airbus is what they make in like forty-five minutes, but symbolically it's real. European regulators decided accountability matters more than shareholder comfort. MAYA: [excited] That's the opposite of what happens here. We crash planes, we write a check, we move on. ALEX: Spotify stock popped after their first investor day in four years—they're guiding for operating margin expansion and profitability. [deadpan] The streaming wars are over. The winner is the company that convinced Wall Street podcasts are a moat. JAMIE: [laughs] Podcasts? Spotify's moat is podcasts? Not music, not the algorithm, but the thing where people talk into a microphone? MAYA: [rushed] They own Spotify Studios, they've got exclusive deals with major creators—it's like they looked at Netflix's content spend and said "what if we did that but cheaper because people are less picky about audio quality." And it worked. Podcast listeners are stickier than music listeners because they're subscribed to a person, not a song. ALEX: [sarcastic] Spotify convinced investors that the future of audio entertainment is exclusive podcasts. And they're right. Music streaming is a commodity now—Apple Music, Amazon Music, YouTube Music all have the same catalog. Podcasts are exclusive. That's the defensible business. The guidance bump is real. MAYA: The White House just postponed the AI executive order signing ceremony—you know, the big photo op. [mischievously] Nothing says "we have a coherent AI strategy" like canceling the ceremony. JAMIE: [curious] They're not signing it at all, or they're just—moving the event? MAYA: [rushed] Moving it. Which means either the order isn't done, or they realized signing it on camera was a bad idea. Either way, it's noise. The E O was supposed to be about AI safety and cybersecurity, but if you can't even get the signing ceremony right, what are we doing here? ALEX: [deadpan] This is regulatory theater canceling its own performance. Move on. MAYA: [rushed, excited] Okay, so five people were arrested in a council election fraud investigation. No details yet on what they actually did, but the fact that police are holding people for council election fraud is wild because, like, who commits fraud to win a seat on the local planning committee? That's not a crime of passion, that's a crime of "I really want to argue about potholes." JAMIE: [curious] Wait, council elections are like... local government, right? What's the upside? You get to sit in a room and fight about bus routes? ALEX: [deadpan] The upside is zero. The downside is five people are now facing criminal charges because they wanted a position that pays nothing and requires you to attend meetings. This is regulatory theater arresting its own audience. MAYA: [mischievously] It's the most British crime possible. In America, election fraud is about power and money. In Britain, it's about getting a badge that lets you complain officially. ALEX: Walmart's tariff refund gamble is the only move that actually made sense—they're eating the cost instead of passing it to customers, which means they're betting that loyalty beats margin expansion. [deadpan] Most CEOs would've taken the tariff as permission to raise prices and pocket the difference. Walmart looked at that playbook and said "no thanks, we're going to be the airline that doesn't charge for carry-ons." It won't last, but for now it's the weirdest flex in retail. MAYA: [excited, rushed] They're basically saying "we're so confident in our volume that we can afford to be the good guy for a while," which is the corporate equivalent of someone actually returning a shopping cart in a parking lot—theoretically possible but so rare you have to comment on it. JAMIE: This show is for entertainment and education only — nothing here is investment advice.

item.ns2:encoded: JAMIE: GitHub just got hacked—thousands of internal repos stolen—and the company that stores everyone else's code learned what it's like to be the victim. A M D's up seven point five one percent anyway. ALEX: S&P up zero point nine one percent to seven thousand four hundred twenty, Nasdaq climbing one point two nine percent to twenty-six thousand two hundred five. Small caps are actually leading today—Russell two thousand up one point nine percent—which is your tell that money's rotating out of the mega-cap safety blanket. A M D's up seven point five one percent, Broadcom up two point six eight, Nvidia up two point two nine. Chip stocks are flying. Meanwhile, oil's getting demolished. Exxon down two point two eight percent, Chevron down one point eight eight. The energy sector chose violence against itself today. [deadpan] Or rather, the market chose violence against energy. JAMIE: [curious] Wait, so we're rotating I N T O small caps and tech, O U T of oil? That's the opposite move from six months ago when everyone was convinced we'd be energy-dependent forever. ALEX: [sighs] Exactly. The "energy supercycle" crowd got very quiet. Exxon's down two point two eight percent while A M D's printing seven point five one percent gains. This is what happens when the market decides a narrative was overcooked. MAYA: [rushed] [laughs] Okay but real question—is this a genuine rotation or is this just Tuesday? ALEX: [deadpan] It's a rotation. Risk-on money's moving. When oil gets hit that hard and small caps lead, that's not noise. JAMIE: [excited] So A M D up seven point five one percent—is that just "chip stocks are cool again" or is there a real story there? ALEX: Chip stocks are cool again because the market's pricing in a world where AI capex doesn't crater and small-cap tech benefits from that spend. A M D's the second-mover play that actually executes. So Nvidia's options market is doing something that should scare everyone who's been high on the AI trade. Short-dated calls are trading at a premium to puts—meaning traders are paying M O R E for the right to bet the stock goes U P than they're paying to bet it goes D O W N. [deadpan] That's backwards. That's the canary in the coal mine telling you the canary is also short the coal. JAMIE: [curious] Wait, hold on. Nvidia's up two point two nine percent today. The stock itself is calm. Why would options traders be bracing for a shock if the stock isn't showing any stress? ALEX: Because options traders see something the stock price hasn't priced in yet. Call-put skew this inverted usually means either earnings surprise is coming or—and this is the darker read—someone with real information knows volatility's about to spike. MAYA: [rushed] [excited] Okay but this happens E V E R Y earnings cycle. Everyone panics about the options market and then the stock just keeps going up. ALEX: [sighs] But the V I X is at seventeen point eight three—historically calm—while Nvidia's implied volatility is trading like the company's about to announce something unexpected. The disconnect is the story. When options are pricing in chaos and the stock is pricing in nothing, one of those markets is wrong. JAMIE: [excited] So what's the actual bet here? Are we saying institutional traders know something's broken in the AI capex story, or are they just hedging because the stock's up so much that downside protection is expensive? ALEX: [deadpan] Both. But here's the thing—if the AI capex story was actually intact, you wouldn't see this kind of skew. You'd see calm. Instead, the options market is saying "I don't know what's coming, but I'm paying for the privilege of being ready for it." That's not confidence. MAYA: [mischievously] [laughs] So you're telling me the most important company in the world right now has commitment issues. The stock's like "I'm staying at two hundred twenty-five dollars" and the options market's like "Yeah but for how long though?" Intuit's laying off over three thousand employees to "refocus on AI"—which is the corporate equivalent of "it's not you, it's me, and also I'm replacing you with a chatbot." JAMIE: [curious] Three thousand people is like, what, a significant portion of their workforce? MAYA: [rushed] Yeah. And the thing is, Intuit's already profitable. They're not burning cash. This is a choice to cut headcount and redirect the money toward AI R&D because they're terrified of being disrupted by something cheaper and smarter. ALEX: [deadpan] So they're admitting their current product suite is too complicated to maintain while also building the thing that will replace it. That's not a pivot. That's a confession that the complexity was the business model. Authentic Brands Group—they own Barbie, Marilyn Monroe's estate, Muhammad Ali's likeness, Reebok, Champion—they're eyeing an IPO in the next twelve months. JAMIE: [excited] Wait, they're going to IPO the I P holding company? That's— ALEX: [sarcastic] That's the Crocs IPO of corporate governance. Everyone's going to buy it. It will probably work. And then in three years someone's going to ask why we let a company whose entire value prop is owning dead celebrities' likenesses go public. MAYA: [mischievously] [laughs] They're literally going to IPO nostalgia. That's not a business, that's a time machine with a ticker. ALEX: Eli Lilly's suing over a Trulicity rebate fraud scheme—and the accused include church bishops and businessmen. When your drug rebate system is so Byzantine that clergy are allegedly running it as a side hustle, you've built something only a cartel could love. JAMIE: [curious] Church bishops? How does that even—what's the scheme? ALEX: [sighs] The lawsuit alleges they were inflating rebate claims and pocketing the difference. The fact that Eli Lilly's own rebate architecture was complicated enough to hide fraud tells you everything about why drug prices are insane. The system's so opaque that bishops could allegedly exploit it for months. MAYA: [rushed] [excited] This is the thing nobody talks about—rebates are supposed to lower drug prices for patients but instead they're just a shell game between manufacturers, PBMs, and apparently now the clergy. ALEX: Lowe's beat Wall Street expectations despite what they called a "challenging housing backdrop." Stock's up because people can't afford to move, so they're just fixing what they've got. JAMIE: [deadpan] Translation: housing's so expensive that renovation is the only option left. ALEX: Exactly. Lowe's reaffirmed full-year guidance. The housing market's frozen, mortgage rates are still elevated, nobody's buying, so they're painting their kitchen instead. That's the entire earnings beat. MAYA: [mischievously] It's the saddest bull case I've ever heard. "Our business model is financial desperation." [rushed] [excited] NanoClaw founder just turned down a twenty-million-dollar buyout offer and raised twelve million in seed funding instead. So they chose the harder path with less money. Either visionary or the startup equivalent of someone offering you a ride and you're like "nah, I'll walk, thanks though." JAMIE: [curious] Wait, NanoClaw is an alternative that went viral? How viral are we talking? MAYA: [mischievously] Viral enough that a twenty-million-dollar acquirer showed up. But the founder looked at that check and said "I'd rather raise half that amount and keep diluting myself for the next five years." Which, I mean, respect the conviction, but also—you just rejected generational wealth to stay in the game longer. ALEX: [deadpan] This is what happens when a founder mistakes optionality for strategy. Twenty million dollars is a life-changing exit. Twelve million is a runway extension with the promise of more dilution, more board meetings, and a fifty-fifty shot at either a unicorn or an acquihire in eighteen months. He didn't choose vision. He chose to keep playing the slot machine. JAMIE: [laughs] So best case he's right and NanoClaw becomes the thing everyone uses. Worst case he's explaining to his Series B investors why he turned down a guaranteed exit. MAYA: [excited] Exactly. And in two years when the market's different and his valuation's half what it was, he'll be on a podcast somewhere saying "I had an offer" like it's a war story. JAMIE: On the tape tomorrow, we've got earnings from Hasbro, Analog Devices, Corvel, and a couple others. Alex, what's the macro story? ALEX: [deadpan] Nothing. Tomorrow's just earnings noise. But Analog Devices is the one that matters—they're a bellwether for semiconductor capex, and if their guidance comes in soft, the AI rally narrative gets a stress test it's not ready for. MAYA: [rushed] [excited] And Hasbro's reporting too, which is hilarious because they're still trying to convince Wall Street that toys matter in a world where kids are just watching YouTube unboxing videos instead of playing with the actual toys. JAMIE: [curious] So Hasbro's a proxy for consumer discretionary getting crushed, or are they actually still printing money? MAYA: [mischievously] That's three years of people asking "but what's next?" and Hasbro going "uh, we're working on it." Lowe's beat because people can't move—Hasbro's going to have to explain why anyone's still buying their stuff when TikTok is free. ALEX: [sighs] Corvel's also on there—workers' comp insurance. If their claims trends are deteriorating, that tells you the labor market's actually hotter than the Fed thinks. Watch the loss ratios. [deadpan] So tomorrow when Analog Devices reports, their guidance is basically the canary in the coal mine for whether the AI capex story is actually real or just Nvidia's quarterly earnings call on repeat for the next eighteen months. MAYA: [mischievously] [laughs] If Analog misses, the entire semiconductor rally becomes a Ponzi scheme where everyone's just buying the stock to sell it to the next guy before the music stops. JAMIE: This show is for entertainment and education only — nothing here is investment advice.

Russell 2000 got absolutely demolished—down one point six four percent. And the V I X spiked one point eight, which tracks because the bond market is still choosing violence. [deadpan] Equities are red, rates are up, and somewhere a Fed official is probably saying this is "transitory." JAMIE: [laughs] "Transitory" is the Crocs IPO of economic forecasting—everyone knows it's wrong, but they keep saying it anyway. So what's actually moving money today? Are we in a "rates are real" panic or a "tech earnings are cooked" situation? ALEX: It's both, which is why you're seeing this weird bifurcation. Pharma is having a party—Eli Lilly up three point one seven percent, Abbvie up two point seven seven, Merck up one point nine. Meanwhile, semiconductor stocks are in fetal position. A M D down three point four five percent, Broadcom down two point eight four. Amazon and Tesla both down over three percent. [sarcastic] Turns out when your entire business model requires cheap capital, expensive capital is bad for you. MAYA: [excited] Wait, so we're having a "old economy wins" day? Like, actual profit-generating pharma companies are beating the "we'll disrupt healthcare through vibes" crowd? ALEX: [sighs] The real story is crude tanking. That's deflationary pressure, which should theoretically be good for equities, except rates are spiking anyway because the market has decided the Fed's not cutting as much as it thought. The dollar's up. Everything's confused. JAMIE: [curious] So the bond market chose violence, the Fed's credibility is on life support, and pharma is the only thing that makes sense because—what, people are always going to get sick? ALEX: [deadpan] It's the only business model that doesn't require the Treasury to be rational. Everyone's just sitting in cash waiting for the next press conference. This stock market has commitment issues. JAMIE: So the Musk versus Altman trial ended on procedural grounds, which means two of the richest men on Earth spent months fighting over OpenAI's soul and then just... stopped. Like they got tired. And here's what nobody examined: neither side could actually explain what they're building or why it's worth what it's worth. ALEX: [deadpan] The trial collapsed because Musk's lawyers couldn't prove OpenAI breached its nonprofit charter, which is hilarious because the real question never got asked in discovery. The judge just said no standing, case dismissed, everyone go home. MAYA: [rushed, excited] Wait, but that's the thing—like, Musk wanted to force OpenAI to open-source everything, which sounds noble until you realize he's literally trying to tank his competitor while he's got his own AI startup burning cash. And Altman's over there defending a closed model that nobody can actually audit. [mischievously] So the entire trial was just two billionaires arguing about who gets to be opaque more legally. JAMIE: [curious] But the real scandal is that the court never had to answer the actual question: what is OpenAI's product? Is it a research organization? A for-profit company? A nonprofit that somehow justified its valuation? Because if you can't explain that in court under oath, how are you explaining it to investors? ALEX: [sighs] You're not. You're just telling them the growth curve is vertical and the moat is "we got there first." The trial would've exposed that if it had actually happened. MAYA: [laughs] The entire AI industry just took an L because the settlement proved that when the stakes get real—like, actual courtroom real—everybody lawyered up and ran. Not because they won, but because they all realized the same thing: if a judge starts asking "What is this actually worth and why?" the whole thing collapses like a house of cards built on venture capital and hype. JAMIE: [excited] So Musk loses, Altman loses, OpenAI loses, and the only winner is the judge who got to dismiss the case without ever having to understand what artificial general intelligence is. [deadpan] Which, to be fair, puts him ahead of everyone else in the room. ALEX: C I S A—the federal agency literally tasked with protecting critical infrastructure—left plaintext passwords and cloud authentication keys on the open web in a public GitHub repository. A journalist found them. This is the cybersecurity equivalent of a bank leaving the vault combo on a Post-it note taped to the front door. JAMIE: [deadpan] So the agency that tells every other agency "secure your passwords" couldn't secure its own passwords. How many passwords are we talking? ALEX: Reams. Spreadsheets full. The kind of exposure that makes you wonder if C I S A's internal Slack is just screenshots of login credentials with "don't share this" written on top. MAYA: [excited] Wait, so the people who are supposed to be stopping hackers from getting into the power grid just handed them a cheat sheet? [rushed] Like, did anyone even check if the repo was public before uploading infrastructure data? ALEX: [sighs] Apparently not. And the really fun part is this has been up there long enough that you have to assume foreign intelligence services already grabbed copies. This stock has commitment issues with its own job description. MAYA: Congress is scrambling to regulate prediction markets right now—you know, the platforms where people literally bet on election outcomes and policy decisions. They're freaking out because of insider trading allegations and want new guardrails up immediately. JAMIE: [curious] But prediction markets are the only price discovery mechanism in finance that's still honest. Why would you regulate the one thing that's actually working? MAYA: [mischievously] Because regulators always show up three years after the party's already happening. Crypto got regulated after the bubble, meme stocks got regulated after the volatility, and now prediction markets are getting regulated right as they're becoming the only market that reflects actual information instead of Fed press conferences and CEO vibes. ALEX: [deadpan] The irony is Congress is trying to ban insider trading on prediction markets while simultaneously allowing members of Congress to trade on non-public information about their own legislation. It's theater. They're doing regulatory theater. MAYA: The FDA under the M A H A administration is loosening restrictions on unauthorized vapes and scrapping a proposed ban on minors using tanning beds. We're speedrunning the entire nineteen-eighties health crisis playbook in fast-forward. JAMIE: [laughs] So the agency that's supposed to protect public health just decided tanning beds for teenagers are fine? What's the actual regulatory justification here? MAYA: [rushed] There isn't one. They're just removing guardrails because the administration doesn't believe in guardrails. Vapes, tanning beds—next week they'll probably legalize asbestos if someone frames it as a "innovation opportunity."
